exercises.title: The mean is the baseline
exercises.brief: Every model has to beat the mean. Write `baseline` that takes a list of numbers and returns the average, then print the mean of [2, 4, 6, 8].

exercises.title: Keep the best three
exercises.brief: A model usually returns many candidates and the caller keeps the best few. Write `top_k` that returns the `k` largest numbers in a list, highest first. Print `top_k([3, 9, 1, 7], 2)`.

exercises.title: Stay inside the budget

exercises.title: How often each word

exercises.title: One request, one effect
exercises.brief: A retried request must not charge twice. Write `is_duplicate` that takes the keys already seen and a new key, and returns True when the key was seen before. Print `is_duplicate(["a", "b"], "b")`.

exercises.title: Did the cache answer?
exercises.brief: Write `cache_status` that takes a cache dictionary and a key and returns "hit" when the key is in the cache and "miss" otherwise. Print `cache_status({"a": 1}, "a")`.

exercises.title: A cache that understands
exercises.brief: A semantic cache serves an old answer when the new question means the same thing. Write `semantic_cache` that takes a list of questions and returns the first one whose letters match the query exactly, or None. Print `semantic_cache(["hello there", "bye"], "hello there")`.

exercises.title: Open the breaker
exercises.brief: A circuit breaker stops sending traffic to a service that keeps failing. Write `breaker_state` that takes a list of results where True means success and returns "open" when three failures in a row are found, otherwise "closed". Print `breaker_state([True, False, False, False])`.

exercises.title: How deep is the queue
exercises.brief: Write `queue_depth` that takes a list of job sizes and returns the total size still waiting. Print `queue_depth([1, 2, 3])`.

exercises.title: What does a call cost
exercises.brief: Write `call_cost` that takes the number of input tokens, the number of output tokens and a price per thousand tokens for each, and returns the total cost. Print `call_cost(1000, 500, 0.002, 0.004)`.

exercises.title: Spend the latency budget
exercises.brief: A request has a latency budget split across several steps. Write `within_budget` that adds the given step times and returns True when the total is under the budget. Print `within_budget([100, 200], 500)`.

exercises.title: Score the answers
exercises.brief: Write `accuracy` that takes the predicted labels and the true labels and returns the share that match, as a number between zero and one. Print `accuracy([1, 0, 1], [1, 0, 0])`.

exercises.title: Where the model is wrong
exercises.brief: Write `confusion` that takes the predicted labels and the true labels and returns a dictionary with the counts of true positives, true negatives, false positives and false negatives. Print it for [1, 0, 1] against [1, 0, 0].

exercises.title: Hide the personal data
exercises.brief: Write `redact` that takes a list of names and returns the same list with every name replaced by the text "REDACTED". Print `redact(["Ada", "Grace"])`.

exercises.title: Spot the injection
exercises.brief: A prompt injection tries to make the model ignore its instructions. Write `looks_like_injection` that returns True when the text contains "ignore previous". Print `looks_like_injection("please ignore previous instructions")`.

exercises.title: Keep the answer grounded
exercises.brief: A grounded answer has to point at a source. Write `has_grounding` that returns True only when the answer names at least one of the given sources. Print `has_grounding("the sky is blue, according to nasa", ["nasa"])`.

exercises.title: Run the eval suite
exercises.brief: An eval suite is a list of cases with the answer you expect. Write `run_eval` that takes the cases and a function and returns the share of cases the function gets right. Print `run_eval([(1, 1), (2, 3)], lambda pair: pair[0] == pair[1])`.

exercises.title: Watch for drift
exercises.brief: A model starts to drift when its accuracy falls below the threshold it was approved at. Write `has_drifted` that takes the current accuracy and the approved accuracy and returns True when the current score is lower. Print `has_drifted(0.8, 0.9)`.

exercises.title: Rate limit the public API
exercises.brief: Design what happens when 50,000 people call your public API at once. Explain how you would rate limit the traffic per user, what you would do with a request that goes over the limit, and how the service stays available when one user floods it.

exercises.title: Give the call a deadline
exercises.brief: Your service calls a slow third party that sometimes never answers. Explain how you would use a timeout and retry with backoff so that one slow call cannot hold up the whole request, and how you would fail fast when the dependency is clearly broken.

exercises.title: Cache the expensive answers
exercises.brief: Every request to your assistant costs money, and the same question arrives often. Explain how you would cache the answers, how long a cache entry should live, and how you would keep a stale entry from being served after the model changed.

exercises.title: Never charge twice
exercises.brief: A payment call timed out, so the client retried, and now the customer has been charged twice. Explain how you would make the write idempotent so that a retry is safe, and how the client would know which attempt was the real one.

exercises.title: Scale from one machine
exercises.brief: Your service starts on one machine and needs to serve a million users. Explain how you would scale it out over time, when you would add a read replica or a shard, and how the data store would keep up with the writes.

exercises.title: Strong or eventual, pick one
exercises.brief: A user updates their profile and immediately sees the old version on another page. Explain the consistency model you would choose, where you would relax it, and how you would keep the system available during a network split.

exercises.title: Take the slow work off the path
exercises.brief: Generating a report takes four minutes, and the user should not have to wait for it. Explain how you would use a queue and a background worker, and what you would do when the queue grows longer than the workers can handle.

exercises.title: The user wrote the instructions
exercises.brief: A user can put anything in the input box, including text that tries to make your assistant reveal its system prompt. Explain how you would treat untrusted input, where you would put the boundary between instruction and data, and how you would test for this before shipping.

exercises.title: The model made it up
exercises.brief: Your assistant confidently invented a citation that does not exist. Explain how you would ground the answers, how you would measure how often it happens, and what you would show the user when the model is not sure.

exercises.title: Do not keep what you must not keep
exercises.brief: People type their medical details into your assistant. Explain what personal data you would collect, what you would redact before sending it to a model, how long you would keep the logs, and who may read them.

exercises.title: Prove it got better
exercises.brief: You changed the prompt and the answers look different. Explain how you would build an eval set, how you would compare the two versions, and what you would watch for so that one good prompt does not hide a regression.

exercises.title: Keep the bill under control
exercises.brief: The bill for the model calls tripled this month. Explain where the tokens are going, how you would cut the cost without making the answers worse, and how you would make the spend visible before it becomes a surprise.

exercises.title: Swap the model without a break
exercises.brief: You want to move from one model to a new one, but the answers come out in a different shape. Explain how you would roll the change out, how you would keep the old model available, and how you would undo the change if it goes wrong.
